instagram_caption:
🚀 The Streaming Ad Boom-to-Bust: the winners moved… and the losers got stuck with bad measurement.

In 2019, streaming advertising was already growing, but the real spark was the “everything gets cheaper to reach audiences” mindset. From 2019 to 2021, YouTube’s video ads climb from about $40B to $56B, while Meta’s video ad engine jumps from ~$30B to ~$58B. Meanwhile, Amazon’s streaming-related ad pull grows from ~$42B to ~$74B—and Disney+ & Hulu stack up inventory fast, going from ~$18B to ~$38B. The chart race at this stage is pure momentum: the platforms that combined reach + creative velocity looked unstoppable.

Then 2022 hits, and the vibe changes. Privacy pressure, attribution gaps, and measurement whiplash turn “growth” into “guesswork.” Google/YouTube holds up relatively well (rising to about $61B), but you can feel the strain in the trendlines. By 2023, Meta drops from ~$71B in 2022 to about ~$60B, and YouTube eases down from ~$61B to ~$58B. This is where the video race gets dramatic: budgets tighten, and advertisers start demanding proof.

Here’s the plot twist: Netflix starts near zero (not reporting streaming ads standalone early), but by 2022 it’s about $2.5B, then jumps to ~$6.8B in 2023, ~$12.6B in 2024, and keeps accelerating into 2026 (about $26B). Disney stays a steady climber—rising to ~$64B in 2023 and ~$73B in 2024—while Amazon stabilizes around the upper-$80s to ~$105B by 2026.

In 2024–2025, the market doesn’t fully “recover”—it re-sorts. The platforms with stronger first-party ecosystems and bundled inventory stabilize faster, while ad effectiveness uncertainty keeps other giants from matching their earlier peak.

facebook_caption:
Streaming advertising didn’t just rise—it underwent a boom-to-bust cycle as privacy and measurement constraints forced advertisers to rethink where ad dollars actually performed. This timeline comparison tracks the direction of major video-ad ecosystems.

From 2019 to 2021, the market shows strong expansion: Meta’s video ads rise from ~$30B to ~$58B, YouTube climbs from ~$40B to ~$56B, Amazon grows from ~$42B to ~$74B, and Disney’s streaming inventory scales from ~$18B to ~$38B. This is the “easy reach” era.

In 2022, uncertainty increases and by 2023 the soft landing becomes visible: Meta declines from ~$71B (2022) to ~$60B (2023), and YouTube slips from ~$61B (2022) to ~$58B (2023). The next phase isn’t a uniform collapse—it’s reallocation. Platforms with better bundled ecosystems and stronger audience signals stabilize.

Netflix adds a dramatic late mover storyline: after effectively starting near $0 in earlier years (standalone ad revenue not reported), its ad-supported scale accelerates from ~$2.5B (2022) to ~$6.8B (2023), ~$12.6B (2024), and an estimated ~$26.0B by 2026. Disney remains consistently upward (to ~$73B in 2024), and Amazon shows resilience, reaching ~$105B by 2026.

threads_caption:
Okay this timeline is WILD. 📉➡️📈

2019–2021 was the streaming-ad boom: Meta goes ~$30B → ~$58B, YouTube ~$40B → ~$56B, Amazon ~$42B → ~$74B, Disney ~$18B → ~$38B.

Then the real turn: 2023 brings the “measurement hangover”—Meta slips ~$71B (2022) → ~$60B (2023) and YouTube ~$61B → ~$58B. Meanwhile Netflix’s ad-supported push goes from basically $0 to ~$26B by 2026 (starting the climb around 2022).

So yeah… the ad dollars didn’t disappear—they moved.
